query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Performing liquid‐metal dealloying of an as-cast, directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor by immersing it in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h creates a bicontinuous, directionally aligned RHEA–Cu composite. In this composite, the formation of nearly pure FCC Cu channels, together with a spontaneous W-rich passivating interlayer at RHEA/Cu interfaces, will yield substantially higher thermal conductivity at elevated temperatures while maintaining mechanical strength and resistance to low-energy He+ irradiation compared to conventional W–Cu composites.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high‐entropy alloy with a single‐BCC, directionally solidified dendrite–interdendrite structure: W/Ta-rich dendrites (~71 vol.%) and connected Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels (~29 vol.%).
generation.intervention: Liquid-metal dealloying by immersing the precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h, which selectively extracts Ti from the interdendritic channels and forms aligned, nearly pure Cu channels with retained RHEA ligaments.
generation.conditions: The composite is produced under the specified reaction conditions (vacuum-sealed in silica at 1200 °C for 96 h) and its performance is evaluated from room temperature up to ~800 °C (and extrapolated above 1000 °C), with irradiation screening using 25 keV He+ implantation up to blistering fluences around 8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2.
generation.structural_mediator: A bicontinuous, directionally aligned architecture consisting of approximately 63.6 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments interwoven with 36.4 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels, with a spontaneously formed ~300 nm thick W-rich passivating interlayer at every RHEA/Cu interface and minor HCP Ti-rich precipitates.
generation.mechanism: During dealloying, Ti (which has a negative heat of mixing with Cu) preferentially dissolves by exchanging with Cu, removing Ti from the interdendritic regions. In contrast, W, Ta, and V remain as RHEA ligaments due to their immiscibility with Cu. The ongoing Ti extraction drives the formation of a W-rich layer at the interface, arresting further exchange. The aligned Cu channels create efficient pathways for lattice-mediated transport, thereby increasing thermal conductivity, while the complex RHEA matrix provides enhanced resistance to He-induced swelling and maintains mechanical durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite is expected to exhibit a substantial improvement in thermal conductivity, especially at high temperature—eventually outperforming pure tungsten. Simultaneously, the mechanically robust and chemically passivated RHEA ligaments should reduce He-induced swelling and blistering relative to pure W and conventional W–Cu composites.
generation.baseline: The performance is compared to the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor, pure tungsten, pure copper, and reported conventional W–Cu composites. The primary irradiation baseline is pure W (with additional comparisons to WTa and WTaV alloys).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is predicted to hold for directionally segregated WTaVTi precursors processed under the 1200 °C/96 h liquid-metal dealloying condition. The thermal conductivity advantage is expected above ~650 °C (with superiority over conventional composites above 1000 °C) and is established under low-energy He+ screening conditions rather than under full neutron irradiation environments.
generation.uncertainty: While the model predicts improved thermal and irradiation performance, uncertainties remain regarding the exact quantitative enhancement of thermal conductivity and the full replication of mechanical durability across a range of load conditions, as well as the translation of low-energy He+ results to other irradiation environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare the composite via liquid-metal dealloying under the specified conditions. Use SEM/TEM-EDS and XRD to confirm phase constitution, directional alignment, and the presence of the ~300 nm W-rich passivating interlayers at the RHEA/Cu interfaces. Measure the temperature-dependent thermal conductivity using laser-flash analysis between room temperature and 800 °C (with extrapolated measurements above 1000 °C). Subject samples to 25 keV He+ implantation up to blistering fluences (≈8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2) and quantify swelling and blister onset with AFM. Perform nanoindentation to assess mechanical performance relative to standard W–Cu composites.
measurements: Phase identification and interface structure via SEM/TEM-EDS and XRD
Temperature-dependent thermal conductivity via laser-flash analysis
Swelling height and blister formation via AFM after 25 keV He+ irradiation
Mechanical hardness and durability via nanoindentation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the resulting composite does not show significantly higher thermal conductivity (especially above ~650 °C) and does not exhibit reduced He-induced swelling and maintained mechanical properties relative to pure tungsten and conventional W–Cu composites, then the hypothesis is rejected.
